analysis.one_liner: Caps the manufacturer price of insulin at $20 per 1,000 units.
analysis.headline: The Insulin for All Act of 2023 was referred to the Senate health committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for insulin manufacturers to charge more than $20 per 1,000 units of insulin — about one-tenth or less of the list prices many patients were paying for a single vial. It applied to all insulin licensed in the United States, in any form: vials, pens, or cartridges. The bill was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day it was introduced in March 2023 and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 8 million-plus Americans who rely on insulin, including people with diabetes who pay list price for vials or pay full cost before meeting their deductible. Sen. Sanders has long cited cases of patients rationing insulin because of its cost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with diabetes who use insulin

how_it_helps.text: Caps what insulin manufacturers can charge at $20 per 1,000 units, across all forms of delivery — vials, pens, and cartridges. [S2] [S3]
The cap applies to all insulin licensed under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act and still marketed, so it covers the brand-name insulins most patients use, not just generics. [S3]
The limit applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' meaning no existing law could override the price cap. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers — principally Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, and Sanofi — would bear the cost, giving up the large gap between their manufacturing costs and the hundreds of dollars a vial they currently charge. The bill does not compensate them or change patent or middleman arrangements.

drawbacks.text: A $20 manufacturer price cap set by statute, with no provision for adjusting to production costs or inflation, could make some insulin products unprofitable to keep making, risking supply shortages unless manufacturers absorb the losses or the law were changed. [S3]

The bill caps only the manufacturer's price; it does not address pharmacy benefit managers, insurers, or pharmacies, so what patients actually pay at the counter would depend on those layers unless competition transmitted the lower price. [S2] [S3]

Drug manufacturers argue price controls reduce the incentive to invest in new formulations and delivery devices; insulin has seen steady innovation in pens and pumps that a hard cap could discourage. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large: insulin is a life-or-death daily medication, and the cap would cut manufacturer prices by roughly 90% from list prices for many products. The main risks are supply and innovation — a hard statutory price floor-low enough could lead some makers to exit, and the bill contains no transition or enforcement mechanism for that problem. On balance, for people who depend on insulin to stay alive, the benefit of an affordable essential drug outweighs those risks, though a better-drafted bill would have addressed the supply question.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee the same day and never got a hearing, a vote, or floor time before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 9, 2023, joined by Sens. Merkley and Markey. [S3]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. [S5]
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors, all Democrats. [S4]
No further action — no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote — was ever recorded, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers came out ahead: they kept selling insulin at hundreds of dollars per vial for another two years, unbound by any price cap. Patients who pay list price are no better off than before the bill was introduced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin makers, who kept high prices

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: Sponsor; member of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap insulin's manufacturer price at $20 per 1,000 units.

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ed Markey
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill on day one.

for.name: Five Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors after introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee chair with power to schedule hearings and markups
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a hearing or committee vote after its referral in March 2023.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor in the two years it was pending.

against.name: Insulin manufacturers
against.role: Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi and the broader pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry opposed government price-setting for its products; insulin makers' list prices remained in the hundreds of dollars per vial.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor was an independent who votes with Democrats, and all 5 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-held committee and majority never moved it.

industries.note: The bill would cap their price at $20 per 1,000 units, far below the hundreds of dollars per vial they charge today. Because insulin is a medication patients cannot skip, their current pricing means many payers — patients, insurers, employers — absorb whatever they charge. [S2] [S3]

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug middlemen
industries.note: The bill caps the manufacturer price only, not what PBMs and other intermediaries add on the way to the patient; it neither removes them nor pays them. A sharp drop in manufacturer prices would shrink the spread they negotiate on. [S2]
